newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI says can't confirm money mkt funds rule report.
newsitem.headline: EMI says can't confirm money mkt funds rule report.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute (EMI) on Thursday said it could not confirm a press report that it was seeking to impose reserve requirements on money market funds after Europe launches its single currency.
The Wall Street Journal Europe reported that officials from the EMI, the forerunner to the future European Central Bank (ECB), had made the proposal at a recent closed meeting in Brussels.

Minimum reserves, much favoured by the Bundesbank and generally opposed by commercial banks, are the percentage of deposits that banks must set aside with their central bank and have become a controversial issue as the euro launch looms.

An EMI spokeswoman could not even confirm that the meeting had taken place but pointed to the EMI's latest report on monetary union preparations, which said the EMI was examining a potential need for a wider definition of the kind of institutions to which reserve requirements would apply.
That would allow the ECB "to subject a broader range of financial institutions than credit institutions alone to reserve requirements."

The German central bank has been urging the ECB to apply reserve requirements when it takes control of monetary policy in the euro area. Lowering or raising reserve requirements effectively influences money supply.

However, as was made clear in its January report, the EMI has left the decision on whether to use reserve ratios at all to the ECB itself, which will not be up and running until 1998, some months ahead of the planned euro launch in January 1999.
The EMI's mandate is to ensure the appropriate mechanisms for a reserve ratio system are in place, should the future central bank opt to apply the instrument.
The EMI's January report, entitled "The single monetary policy in stage three: Specification of the operational framework," made the following points on minimum reserves:

"According to Article 19.1 of the Statute of the ESCB (European System of Central Banks), the ECB may require credit institutions to hold minimum reserves on accounts with the NCBs (national central banks) within the framework of the ESCB's minimum reserve system."
"In considering the efficiency of a potential minimum reserve system, the ECB might need to impose reserve ratios on a broad range of liabilities and institutions.

"Therefore the EMI has seen a need to study further the extension of the definition of Article 19.1 so as to allow the ECB to subject a broader range of financial institutions than credit institutions alone to reserve requirements."
The report added that the ECB would have to apply to the EU Council to set a legal framework for a minimum reserve system after its establishment.
